what_it_does: Graph neural networks (GNNs) learn by passing messages along the edges of a graph — think of modeling a social network where each person updates their representation based on their friends' representations. Billion-node graphs (like a social network or a web graph) cannot fit in one machine's memory, so researchers split them into partitions processed one at a time. The snag is that real-world graphs follow a power law: a tiny fraction of nodes have enormous numbers of connections (think celebrity accounts), and naively partitioning such graphs puts those super-connected nodes into one partition, causing memory to overflow. Buffalo assigns nodes to 'buckets' — a flexible grouping that can spread a super-connected node's neighbors across multiple non-adjacent buckets — preventing any single bucket from becoming too large. It also includes a fast lightweight formula that predicts how much memory a proposed partition will use before committing to it, and uses random graph sampling to reduce the expensive work of preparing each batch of data for training.
